meta.title: Mouse-mass evidence: Zaunkoenig zero-gram claim + empirical studies
meta.bottom_line: Zaunkoenig's "zero grams" is an argued design philosophy (2018 blog, no experiment), not research data. The empirical studies cover 40-190 g only. The largest gaming study (n=72) found 50, 60 and 90 g all beat 100 g by similar margins (a threshold, not a slope); a small study (n=12) found its 40 g mouse had the highest error rate and 60 g was preferred. Nothing has been tested in the 20-40 g range where Theseus (29 g) sits. Honest slide wording: "Lighter beat heavier down to the lightest mass tested (50 g, n=72). Below 40 g there is no published data; Zaunkoenig argues the optimum is zero. We will publish our own test."

claim_quote.value: The optimal weight of a gaming mouse therefore is zero grams.
claim_quote.source_title: Zaunkoenig blog, "Optimal weight of a gaming mouse", 29 Dec 2018, Dominik & Patrick Schmalzried
claim_quote.label: MC
claim_quote.note: Section heading on the same page: "The optimal weight of a gaming mouse is zero grams". The page is the original source.

zaunkoenig.authors: Dominik Schmalzried and Patrick Schmalzried (Zaunkoenig founders)

method.value: Argument from inertia and motor control, plus the Colin Chapman quote "Adding power makes you faster on the straights; subtracting weight makes you faster everywhere." No experiment, participants or measurements are reported.
method.source_title: Zaunkoenig blog, "Optimal weight of a gaming mouse", 29 Dec 2018, Dominik & Patrick Schmalzried
method.label: MC

supporting_quotes.value: Think of added mouse weight as built-in latency.
supporting_quotes.source_title: Zaunkoenig blog, "Optimal weight of a gaming mouse", 29 Dec 2018, Dominik & Patrick Schmalzried
supporting_quotes.label: MC

supporting_quotes.value: Put another way: the heavier your mouse, the more often you will miss your targets.
supporting_quotes.source_title: Zaunkoenig blog, "Optimal weight of a gaming mouse", 29 Dec 2018, Dominik & Patrick Schmalzried
supporting_quotes.label: MC
supporting_quotes.note: Asserted, not measured. Yan et al. 2022 (n=12) found the 40 g mouse had the highest error rate, which does not support a monotonic version of this claim at the low end.

supporting_quotes.value: If you want high control over your aiming, nothing beats a very light mouse plus a slow mousepad and slow mouse feet.
supporting_quotes.source_title: Zaunkoenig blog, "Optimal weight of a gaming mouse", 29 Dec 2018, Dominik & Patrick Schmalzried
supporting_quotes.label: MC

supporting_quotes.value: At Zaunkoenig, we strongly believe that the optimal weight of a gaming mouse is zero grams. With 23 grams for the M1K we got pretty close, but there are still 23 grams to go.
supporting_quotes.source_title: Zaunkoenig blog, "M1K weight in review", 31 Aug 2020, Dominik Schmalzried
supporting_quotes.label: MC

m1k_production_weight.unit: g, mean of the first 333 units (regular bottom shell); most between 22.5 and 24.3 g
m1k_production_weight.source_title: Zaunkoenig blog, "M1K weight in review", 31 Aug 2020, Dominik Schmalzried
m1k_production_weight.label: MC
m1k_production_weight.note: manufacturer weighed every unit; not independent

zaunkoenig.how_to_cite_on_slide: Zaunkoenig (makers of the 23 g M1K and M2K) argue the optimal mouse weight is zero grams: "The optimal weight of a gaming mouse therefore is zero grams." (zaunkoenig.co, 29 Dec 2018). Label it as an argument [MC], not a study.

studies.citation: Conroy, Toth & Campbell 2022, "The effect of computer mouse mass on target acquisition performance among action video gamers", Applied Ergonomics 99:103637, doi:10.1016/j.apergo.2021.103637
studies.label: IM
studies.task: target acquisition task (FPS composite skill); mice varied only by mass; two control-display gains

results.value: participants were 4% faster and 9% more accurate with 50 g, 60 g and 90 g mice compared to the 100 g mouse
results.source_title: Conroy, Toth & Campbell 2022, "The effect of computer mouse mass on target acquisition performance among action video gamers", Applied Ergonomics 99:103637, doi:10.1016/j.apergo.2021.103637
results.label: IM

results.value: 34% more accurate and 14% more precise when using lower control-display gain
results.source_title: Conroy, Toth & Campbell 2022, "The effect of computer mouse mass on target acquisition performance among action video gamers", Applied Ergonomics 99:103637, doi:10.1016/j.apergo.2021.103637
results.label: IM

results.value: preferred lighter mice (50 g and 60 g) when performing the skill at a lower control-display gain
results.source_title: Conroy, Toth & Campbell 2022, "The effect of computer mouse mass on target acquisition performance among action video gamers", Applied Ergonomics 99:103637, doi:10.1016/j.apergo.2021.103637
results.label: IM

studies.reading: The benefit appears between 90 g and 100 g with no reported gain from 90 to 50 g in the abstract; lightest tested 50 g. Full-text effect sizes per mass not extracted in this pass.

studies.citation: Yan, Joshi, Barr & Harris Adamson 2022, "The impact of computer mice weight on muscle activity, performance, and user preferences while gaming", Proc. HFES Annual Meeting 66(1):868-870, doi:10.1177/1071181322661516
studies.label: IM
studies.task: Fitts' test + gaming tasks; wireless surface EMG; discomfort and preference ratings

results.value: muscle activity was slightly lower when using the heaviest mouse (140g); differences were not statistically significant
results.source_title: Yan, Joshi, Barr & Harris Adamson 2022, "The impact of computer mice weight on muscle activity, performance, and user preferences while gaming", Proc. HFES Annual Meeting 66(1):868-870, doi:10.1177/1071181322661516
results.label: IM

results.value: The lightest mouse (40g) had the highest error rate.
results.source_title: Yan, Joshi, Barr & Harris Adamson 2022, "The impact of computer mice weight on muscle activity, performance, and user preferences while gaming", Proc. HFES Annual Meeting 66(1):868-870, doi:10.1177/1071181322661516
results.label: IM

results.value: The 60g mouse received the highest overall preference score
results.source_title: Yan, Joshi, Barr & Harris Adamson 2022, "The impact of computer mice weight on muscle activity, performance, and user preferences while gaming", Proc. HFES Annual Meeting 66(1):868-870, doi:10.1177/1071181322661516
results.label: IM

studies.reading: Small sample, conference paper. The only study found that tested 40 g; it does not support "lighter is always better" below ~60 g.

studies.citation: Wang, Li, Arippa, Barr, Xue & Harris-Adamson 2023, "The effects of mouse weight and connection type on performance, muscle activity, and preferences among professional gamers", Int. J. Industrial Ergonomics 97:103493, doi:10.1016/j.ergon.2023.103493
studies.label: IM
studies.task: four mice differing in weight and connection type

results.value: No statistically significant differences between mouse weight were found.
results.source_title: Wang, Li, Arippa, Barr, Xue & Harris-Adamson 2023, "The effects of mouse weight and connection type on performance, muscle activity, and preferences among professional gamers", Int. J. Industrial Ergonomics 97:103493, doi:10.1016/j.ergon.2023.103493
results.label: IM

results.value: The wireless mouse had a lower error rate (p = 0.05) and a higher overall comfort rating (p = 0.01).
results.source_title: Wang, Li, Arippa, Barr, Xue & Harris-Adamson 2023, "The effects of mouse weight and connection type on performance, muscle activity, and preferences among professional gamers", Int. J. Industrial Ergonomics 97:103493, doi:10.1016/j.ergon.2023.103493
results.label: IM

studies.reading: 7 g difference too small to detect with n=16. Useful for the wireless-vs-wired slide.

studies.citation: Chen, Lee & Cheng 2012, "The weight of computer mouse affects the wrist motion and forearm muscle activity during fast operation speed task", Eur. J. Applied Physiology 112(6):2205-2212, doi:10.1007/s00421-011-2198-3
studies.label: IM
studies.task: office point-and-click between two targets at 50/min and 25/min; EMG of ECR, ECU, ED, upper trapezius; electrogoniometer

results.value: The wrist movement range and the forearm muscle activities showed a V-shape tendency with the lowest value in the mouse weight of 130 g. This tendency was diminished during the slow speed tasks.
results.source_title: Chen, Lee & Cheng 2012, "The weight of computer mouse affects the wrist motion and forearm muscle activity during fast operation speed task", Eur. J. Applied Physiology 112(6):2205-2212, doi:10.1007/s00421-011-2198-3
results.label: IM

studies.reading: Office task with office-weight mice, not gaming; shows muscle cost is not monotonic in mass. Do not over-apply to 29 g.

example.source_title: Duarte, BMC notebook "Body segment parameters": Dempster via Winter (2009) and Zatsiorsky adjusted by de Leva (1996) mass fractions
example.label: DV
example.formula: hand = 0.006 x body mass; share = m_mouse / (m_hand + m_mouse): 60/(420+60)=12.5%, 29/(420+29)=6.5%
example.note: For wrist/arm-driven flicks the hand moves too, so cutting 31 g removes ~6% of the moving mass; for finger-driven micro-corrections the mouse is a larger share (no finger-mass source found). Body masses are illustrative, not sourced.

physics_context.newton: F = m*a: at the same acceleration, the force your hand must add to move the mouse scales with mouse mass; at 29 g that extra force is 48% of a 60 g mouse's (29/60) [DV].
